endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: (d) the AI Services, AI Training Data, and Outputs have been assessed for bias, inaccuracies, unfairness, and controls, mechanisms, and policies are in place to mitigate and ensure the elimination of same.

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: The AI governance structure does not need to be its own standalone team but should be responsible for aiding in the risk-based management of third-party and internally developed AI tools or AI-embedded tools, including selection, implementation, risk management, lifecycle management, compliance, and oversight, as appropriate.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Identify any personnel responsible for assessing sufficiency of third-party systems or components, and determine whether processes are in place for third parties to report potential vulnerabilities, risks, or biases in the AI system.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether convening a multidisciplinary negotiating team with an accountable owner, preset walk-away terms, and legal review produces AI vendor contracts with stronger protections. Three governance frameworks endorse related practices, so the recommendation currently rests on expert consensus rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard of unprepared negotiation. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The three endorsements are expert guidance, and their agreement shows consensus on intent rather than evidence that the practice changes contract terms or patient outcomes.

One CHAI playbook lists bias and accuracy assessment as a must-level contract condition, and the RUAIH guidance assigns vendor selection and compliance to the governance structure. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks organizations to name personnel who assess third-party systems. None of these sources specifies negotiation terms or walk-away criteria, and no study evaluates them.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI vendor contracts negotiated with and without a prepared multidisciplinary team and legal review. Useful measures would include the presence of audit rights, bias and performance reporting clauses, data-use limits, and liability terms, along with later incidents, disputes, or termination events tied to contract gaps.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have less legal and procurement staff to form such a team, and the absence of evidence leaves unknown whether the practice is feasible for them or whether contract protections reach the patients they serve.
